messages.subject: Error:  No matches for function name="multiply"
parts:
Hello,

Trying to setup a fairly simple mixed effects regression as part of my learning about stan.  VERY simple linear regression where the slope varies by group.

I get a weird error when trying to compile this model.

Would anyone be able to tell me what I'm doing wrong here.

Thanks!

=====================================================
DIAGNOSTICS FROM PARSER:

no matches for function name="multiply"
    arg 0 type=real[1]
    arg 1 type=real
no matches for function name="add"
    arg 0 type=int
    arg 1 type=ill formed
no matches for function name="multiply"
    arg 0 type=real[1]
    arg 1 type=real
no matches for function name="add"
    arg 0 type=ill formed
    arg 1 type=ill formed
expression is ill formed
Parser expecting: <eps>
=====================================================


Model is below:

=====================================================

data {
    int N; // number of tracts
    int n_class; // number of groups

    real y[N];
    int class[N]; 
    real var_1[N];
    real var_2[N];
   
}
parameters {

    real class_effect[n_class];

    real b_var_1[N];
    real b_var_2[N];

    real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_class_effect;
    real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_var_1;
    real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_var_2;

    real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma_regression;
   
}

model {

    real mu[N];

    b_var_1 ~ normal(0, sigma_var_1);
    b_var_2 ~ normal(0, sigma_var_2);
   
    for(j in 1:n_class){
        class_effect[j] ~ normal(0, sigma_class_effect);
    }


    for(i in 1:N){

        mu[i] <- 1 + class_effect[class[N]] + b_var_1 * var_1[i]  + b_var_2 * var_2[i];
       
        y[i] ~ normal(mu[i], sigma_regression);

    }
}

=====================================================

Sorry about this -- we're working hard to get the
next Stan release ready. Version 1.0.3 broke the
location reporting for error messages.

The first problem with the model is that
"class" is a reserved word. So I changed "class" to "clazz"
(it's the usual replacement because "class" is reserved
in C++ and in Java), which highlighted the real error:


INVALID COMMAND-LINE ARGUMENT
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=../temp2/noah.stan; line=41, column=87

mu[i] <- 1 + clazz_effect[clazz[N]] + b_var_1 * var_1[i] + b_var_2 * var_2[i];
^-- here


DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

no matches for function name="multiply"
arg 0 type=real[1]
arg 1 type=real
no matches for function name="add"
arg 0 type=real

arg 1 type=ill formed
no matches for function name="multiply"
arg 0 type=real[1]
arg 1 type=real
no matches for function name="add"
arg 0 type=ill formed
arg 1 type=ill formed
expression is ill formed
Parser expecting: <eps>

The problem is that we don't have scalar-array mulitplication.
So trying to mulitply an array (b_var_2) by a scalar
(var_2[i]) is undefined.

If you change the array types to vector types, the arithmetic
should work as you expect. For instance, change the declaration

real b_var_2[N];

to

vector[N] b_var_2;

The I/O is the same for both, so you shouldn't see any difference
in the model itself.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Error:  No matches for function name="multiply"
parts:
On Monday, December 10, 2012 1:54:17 PM UTC-5, Noah wrote:
Would anyone be able to tell me what I'm doing wrong here.

DIAGNOSTICS FROM PARSER:

no matches for function name="multiply"
    arg 0 type=real[1]
    arg 1 type=real
This is the clue: multiplication is not defined for two things you want to multiply. In particular,
mu[i] <- 1 + class_effect[class[N]] + b_var_1 * var_1[i]  + b_var_2 * var_2[i];

b_var_1 and b_var_2 are of length N. You presumably intended for b_var_1 and b_var_2 to be scalars or maybe meant to write b_var_1[i] * var_1[i] + b_var_2[i] * var_2[i]. Also, class[N] should presumably be class[i]. Also, as of Stan v1.0.4, you won't be able to declare and use a variable called class because that is a reserved word in C++, but you could declare and use a variable called Class. Also, doing a model like this the BUGS way will be slow and inefficient in Stan.

Ben

>

> b_var_1 and b_var_2 are of length N. You presumably intended for b_var_1 and b_var_2 to be scalars or maybe meant to
> write b_var_1[i] * var_1[i] + b_var_2[i] * var_2[i]. Also, class[N] should presumably be class[i]. Also, as of Stan
> v1.0.4, you won't be able to declare and use a variable called class because that is a reserved word in C++, but you
> could declare and use a variable called Class. Also, doing a model like this the BUGS way will be slow and inefficient
> in Stan.

Ben -- I didn't read past the first syntax bug, nor do I
see anything that looks hugely inefficient in the model
other than vectorization of the normals.

It could certainly be made faster by:

1. vectorizing the normals, as in replacing

for(j in 1:n_clazz)
class_effect[j] ~ normal(0, sigma_class_effect);

with

class_effect ~ normal(0, sigma_class_effect);

2.a. getting rid of the intermediate variable mu in the regression,
replacing

real mu[N];
...
for (i in 1:N) {
mu[i] <- 1 + class_effect[clazz[N]] + b_var_1 * var_1[i] + b_var_2 * var_2[i];

y[i] ~ normal(mu[i], sigma_regression);
}

with

for (i in 1:N)
y[i] ~ normal(1 + class_effect[clazz[N]] + b_var_1 * var_1[i] + b_var_2 * var_2[i],
sigma_regression);

but I doubt you'll even be able to notice the speedup from that.

2.b. vectorizing the normal by allocating a vector of means instead:

real mu[N];
...
for (i in 1:N)
mu[i] <- 1 + class_effect[clazz[N]] + b_var_1 * var_1[i] + b_var_2 * var_2[i];

y ~ normal(mu, sigma_regression);


3. You can also rescale, the class effects, replacing

for (j in 1:n_class)
class_effect[j] ~ normal(0, sigma_class_effect);

with

for (j in 1:n_class)
class_effect_raw[j] ~ normal(0,1);

vector[n_class] class_effect;
class_effect <- class_effect_raw * sigma_class_effect;

You'll need to make class_effect_raw[j] the parameter vector (not
an array, so you can do the vector-scalar multiplication) and
make class_effect[j] a transformed parameter. Or you can
make class_effect[j] local or just replace its use with
(class_effect_raw[j] * sigma_class_effect.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error:  No matches for function name="multiply"
parts:
On 12/10/12 2:50 PM, Noah Silverman wrote:

> Didn't know about the reserved variable. Good catch!

The reserved word list is in the 1.0.3 doc, but the
parser wasn't trapping uses. In 1.0.4, the stanc parser
will catch the reserved words and report them as errors.
(Otherwise you'd just get errors when trying to compile the
C++ generated by Stan, which we want to eliminate so that
Stan users never ever have to think about C++.)

> 1) I thought that the betas of a model are scaler, and that we just sample them repeatedly from the posterior. (At least
> that's how it appears with bugs/jags.)

I'm not sure what you mean by "betas of a model" -- you don't
have variables named "beta", so I assume you mean what
you declared as arrays, b_var_1 and b_var_2.

The problem is that Stan doesn't support

real x[N];
real y[N];
real c;

y <- x * c; // ILL FORMED

It does support:

vector[N] x;
vector[N] y;
real c;

y <- x * c; // OK
> 2) You mentioned that my structure will be "slow and inefficient" in stan. Is there a faster/better way?

See my follow up message. Ben may have other ideas.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error:  No matches for function name="multiply"
parts:
On Monday, December 10, 2012 2:50:34 PM UTC-5, Noah wrote:
Ben,

A bit confused.

1) I thought that the betas of a model are scaler, and that we just sample them repeatedly from the posterior. (At least that's how it appears with bugs/jags.)

I meant that you might have intended there to be one coefficient for var_1 and one coefficient for var_2. Or maybe you meant the coefficients to vary by class or something. What you wrote was that there is one coefficient for each observation on var_1 and var_2. That is technically legal, but it is a weird model.
2) You mentioned that my structure will be "slow and inefficient" in stan.  Is there a faster/better way?

Similar to what I said about the count model you were doing before: vectorize as much as possible and Matt trick. Or see what Bob said. This is how I would have done it (with scalar coefficients, using matrix algebra would be a little faster and more general):

data {
    int N; // number of tracts
    int n_class; // number of groups

    real y[N];

int Class[N];
    real var_1[N];
    real var_2[N];
    real<lower=0> sigma_var_1; // need to specify prior sd
    real<lower=0> sigma_var_2; // ditto
}
parameters {

    vector[n_class] class_effect_z;
    real b_var_1;
    real b_var_2;

    real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_class_effect;
    real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma_regression;
   
}
transformed parameters { // Matt trick
    vector[n_class] class_effect;
    class_effect <- sigma_class_effect * class_effect_z;
}
model {
    vector[N] mu;

    b_var_1 ~ normal(0,sigma_var_1);
    b_var_2 ~ normal(0,sigma_var_2);
    class_effect_z ~ normal(0,1); // implies class_effect ~ normal(0,sigma_class_effect)


    for(i in 1:N){
        mu[i] <- 1 + class_effect[Class[i]] + b_var_1 * var_1[i]  + b_var_2 * var_2[i];
    }
    y ~ normal(mu, sigma_regression); // pulled out of loop
}

Ben

Thanks!!!
